## **Prepared For:**

## **Executive Summary**

Construction for the Munnsville Wind Farm (project) in Madison and Oneida Counties, New York was completed on November 1, 2007.  The project is a 34.5 megawatt (MW) wind farm.  The 23 GE 1.5 sle turbines have a maximum height of 119 meters (m; 389 feet [ft]) (tower and blade-tip height combined).  Seven of the 23 turbines are lit with FAA approved lighting.

In accordance with the State Environmental Quality Review (SEQR) Negative Declaration and the Environmental Assessment Form for the project, post-construction monitoring was conducted during the first year following construction by Stantec Consulting (Stantec) on behalf of E.ON Climate and Renewables (E.ON).  The purpose of the mortality study was to investigate avian and bat mortality at the wind farm, the rate of mortality, and the possible causes of mortality.  It was the purpose of the breeding bird displacement study to investigate the level of impact to breeding birds due to development and operation of the wind farm.  The postconstruction monitoring efforts, targeting potential avian and bat mortality and breeding bird displacement, was developed in 2005.  The Town of Stockbridge Planning Board served as the lead agency overseeing the project and the wildlife monitoring protocols, and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) and New York State Department of Environmental Conservation (NYSDEC) provided recommendations regarding the wildlife monitoring protocols.  It was determined that the bird and bat mortality study protocol would follow established and accepted procedures for monitoring collision mortality (including searches under turbines and analysis of scavenging and searcher efficiency).  The study would take place during the first year following construction of the project, and the need for additional years of survey would be dependent on the results of Year 1.  It was determined that the breeding bird displacement survey would be conducted during the first and fifth year following construction.

## _Bird and Bat Mortality Study_

The bird and bat mortality surveys were conducted from April 15 to November 15, 2008.  The mortality surveys consisted of weekly standardized searches at 12 of the 23 turbines (52 percent).  Two of the original turbines included in searches were excluded from the study midseason (after consultation with a NYSDEC biologist) in order to incorporate two different turbines that allowed for greater visibility during searches; regardless, 12 turbines total were searched once each week.  Standardized searches consisted of surveying transects established every 5 m (16 ft) within 120 m by 120 m (393 ft by 393 ft) plots centered around each search turbine.  Turbines included in the searches were chosen based on a random-stratified habitat approach.  Searcher efficiency and scavenger carcass removal trials were conducted on a seasonal basis (spring, summer, and fall).  Additional monitoring effort included supplemental dog searches to validate the results of standard searches, bat acoustic monitoring adjacent to turbines included in mortality searches, and documentation of incidental wildlife observations that occurred in the proximity the turbines.

During surveys, any intact carcasses or evidence of scavenged birds or bats found were documented and collected.  The results of dog searches were kept separate from those of standard weekly searches and a different estimate of annual mortality was calculated based on both datasets.  Additional fatalities found by surveyors outside of the standardized searches were recorded as incidental findings and were not included in the estimates of total mortality. The number of carcasses found during standard searches and dog searches, searcher efficiency rates, scavenger removal rates, and the proportion of towers searched were used to determine two annual estimates of total bird and bat mortality, an estimate of bird and bat mortality per turbine per year, and an estimate of bird and bat mortality per MW per year.

Of 10 total bird fatalities found, 5 were found during standard weekly searches, 3 were found during dog searches (the remains of a scavenged red-tailed hawk were found in two different places, 1 wing was discovered during a standard search and another part of the carcass was found later that same morning during a dog search[1] ), and three birds were found incidentally. Forty percent of bird species (n=4) found during standard surveys, incidental findings, and during dog searches consisted of passerine species (rock pigeon, ruby-crowned kinglet, redeyed vireo, and song sparrow).  The three large game birds (wild turkeys) found represent thirty percent of avian fatalities, and the two raptors found (red-tailed hawks) represent twenty percent of the avian fatalities.

Of 10 total bats found, 5 were found during dog searches; 4 were found during standard surveys, and one hoary bat was found incidentally.  Hoary bat (n=6) represented 60 percent of bats found during fatality searches; little brown bat (n=2) represented 20 percent of bat fatalities; and big brown (n=1) and eastern red bat (n=1) each accounted for 10 percent of bat fatalities.

During the study, searcher efficiency trials were conducted during each season.  A total of 12 bird carcasses were placed during trials, of which the surveyor found four for a searcher efficiency rate of 33 percent.  Seven of 11 bats placed were recovered for a searcher efficiency rate of 64 percent.  The results of the dog searcher efficiency trial indicated that for 3 birds placed, the surveyor with the dog recovered 2 (67 percent).  For two bats placed, both were recovered by the surveyor with the dog (100 percent).

A scavenger carcass removal trial was conducted every season during the search period.  A total of 21 birds and 4 bats were placed during the carcass removal trials.  On day 4 (the average period between potential impact and discovery during weekly intervals), 57 percent of bird carcasses (n=12) remained detectable for the surveyor.  On day 14, 38 percent of bird carcasses (n=8) remained visible to the surveyor.  On day 4, 75 percent of bat carcasses (n=3) remained detectable for the surveyor.  One of 4 bats, 25 percent of trial carcasses, remained on day 14.

The weekly surveys resulted in an estimated total of 51.12 bird fatalities per year (± 25.55), with 2.22 birds/turbine/year and 1.48 birds/MW/year.  The estimated total number of bat fatalities was 16.02 per year (± 6.50), with 0.70 bats/turbine/year and 0.46 bats/MW/year.

Based on dog searches, the estimate of bird fatalities is 39.28 birds per year (± 20.38), with 1.71 birds/turbine/year, and 1.14 birds/MW/year; and an estimated total of 66.67 bats per year (± 46.45), with 2.90 bats/turbine/year, and 1.93 bats/MW/year.

Due to the overall low sample size of bird and bat fatalities, statistical relationships among landscape and other turbine design variables are not powerful.  However, there were some trends observed during the statistical analysis for all detected bird and bat fatalities (including those found during standard weekly searches, seasonal dog searches, and those found incidentally combined):

- Bird and bat fatalities occurred at turbines located in a variety of ground cover types within search plots.

- When looking at the number of bird and bat fatalities found at turbines with variable search plot areas, as the search area increased the number of bird fatalities found decreased; however, there was no statistical relationship between the size of search area at turbines and the number of fatalities found at turbines.

- There was no statistical relationship between the number of bird and bat fatalities found at turbines located at variable elevations within the wind farm.

- While there was no statistical difference between bird fatalities found at turbines bordered by forest edge and turbines in open landscapes, there was a difference between bird fatalities at turbines bordered by forest edge and turbines with a partial forest edge.  There was no statistical difference in the number of bat fatalities at each of these landscape settings.

- There was no statistical difference in the number of bird and bat fatalities found at turbines located in proximity of wetlands verses those turbines not located in the proximity of wetlands.

- There was no statistical difference in the number of bird and bat fatalities found at lit verses unlit turbines.

The temporal analysis of bird and bat fatalities indicated observable trends:

- Bird fatalities were believed to occur predominantly during small-scale and localized resident bird movements due to the nature of species involved in collisions; and

- The majority of bats were found during the late-summer/fall survey period (mid-July to end of August).

There were no federally or state listed avian or bat species found during fatality searches.  The results of post-construction monitoring during the first year of operation suggest that the Munnsville Wind Farm presents collision mortality for birds and bats; however, the rate of mortality is relatively low for both birds and bats with no unreasonable adverse impacts.

## _Breeding Bird Displacement Study_

A pre-construction breeding bird study was conducted in 2005 by Curry and Kerlinger, LLC (Kerlinger and Dowdell 2005).  It was determined that the post-construction methods would, in part, follow those of the pre-construction methods in order to compare species diversity and abundance among the survey years.

It was the purpose of the post-construction breeding bird displacement study to investigate the level of impact to breeding birds due to development and operation of the wind farm.  Impacts to breeding birds could include displacement from habitat as measured by decreased species diversity, a decrease in the number of breeding individuals, and decreased relative abundance of breeding birds in the vicinity of the operating turbines.  Post-construction surveys also targeted the continued occurrence of state species of conservation concern including horned lark (special concern), northern harrier (threatened), and vesper sparrow (special concern) as these species were detected on-site during the pre-construction surveys.

Breeding bird point count surveys were conducted during three separate site visits in 2008: May 28 and 29; June 16 and 17; and June 26 and 27.  A total of 21 breeding bird point count locations were surveyed.  A total of 1,061 individual birds were observed during the 3 site visits at all point counts combined.  Sixty-seven different species were observed.  An additional 6 species were observed incidentally while biologists were on-site between point count surveys or during the mortality searches, for a total of 73 species observed.

There were a number of species for which the overall number of individuals (as well as their frequency among survey points) was lower, by more than a few individuals, than detected during pre-construction surveys.  Forest, forest edge, and grassland species showed declines in the number of individuals during post-construction surveys at survey points in the vicinity of turbines as well as at non-turbine survey points.  There were a few species for which a greater

number of individuals (and generally a greater frequency among points) was detected during the post-construction surveys than during pre-construction surveys.

When comparing turbine and reference sites in the same habitats, breeding bird displacement was observed at turbines located at forest edge habitats, but was not observed at turbines in agricultural settings.  Restoration of habitat or habituation of forest edge dwelling species during the fifth year of operation may result in more comparable species diversity and relative abundance at turbine and reference sites; however, some displacement may be long-term due to permanent clearing during project construction at a few turbines.

There were observations of northern harrier, horned lark, and vesper sparrow (among other species of conservation concern) that were observed on-site during the 2008 post-construction surveys.  These observations suggest these three species are generally not avoiding the Project area.  Many of the observation locations of these species were similar to those in 2005, with the exception of vesper sparrow which was detected in only one location in 2008, but in 14 different locations during the 2005 pre-construction surveys (Kerlinger and Dowdell 2005).  There are stochastic factors that likely influenced the number of individual birds observed among survey points during 2005 and 2008.  Such factors as the natural variation in local bird populations among years, variable landowner management practices among years, and the fact that certain species make less frequent or less conspicuous calls and may not be detected during all surveys at a sample point should be considered when evaluating the 2005 and 2008 datasets.

## **1.0 Introduction**

Birds and bats are known to collide with tall man-made structures including communication towers, buildings, and wind turbines.  Emerging evidence suggests that bats may be at greatest risk of collision during periods of low cloud cover and calm wind speeds, often after the passing of storm fronts (Kunz _et al._ 2007).  Nocturnally migrating birds may be at greater risk of collision with tall structures when weather conditions reduce visibility (Crawford 1981; Avery _et al._ 1976, 1977).

A review of existing mortality studies indicated that bat mortality in the U.S. ranged from 0 to 63.9 bats per turbine per year (bats/turbine/year) (Kerlinger 2002, 2006; GAO 2005; Arnett 2005; Fiedler _et al._ 2007).  The Buffalo Mountain facility in Tennessee observed rates among the highest reported in the U.S. at 63.9 bats/turbine/year (1,149 total bats) (Fiedler _et al._ 2007). Locations in the Appalachian Mountains observed mortality as high as 38 bats/turbine during a 6-week study period (1,364 to 1,980 total bats) (Arnett 2005).  Another recent study in New York documented 15.54 to 18.53 bats/turbine/year (3,030 to 3,614 total bats) (Jain _et al._ 2008). Raptor mortality in the U.S. has been low at wind farms with modern turbine models, ranging from 0 to 0.41 raptors/turbine/year (Erickson _et al._ 2002, GAO 2005, Jain _et al._ 2008). Nocturnal migrant songbird fatalities at most existing wind farms have also been relatively low, despite the high reported number of collisions of nocturnal migrants with large, lit and guyed communication towers (typically greater than 153 meters [m; 500 feet {ft}]) in the U.S. (Jain _et al._ 2007).  The number of reported songbird fatalities associated with wind farms in the U.S. has ranged from 0 to 9.48 fatalities/turbine/year (GAO 2005, National Research Council 2007, Jain _et al._ 2007, Jain _et al._ 2008).

There is limited data available from wind sites regarding displacement impacts to birds in grassland and agricultural settings.  One study conducted at the Buffalo Ridge facility in Minnesota indicated a decreased bird density and diversity in turbine plots as opposed to reference plots (NRC 2007, Osborn _et al._ 1998).  Limited breeding bird displacement studies have been conducted at wind facilities in forested habitats in the eastern U.S.  Breeding bird surveys were conducted prior to construction, during construction, and after construction at the Green Mountain Power Corporation’s Wind Power Facility in Searsburg, Vermont.  The same diversity of species was detected during the three survey periods; however, the abundance and frequency of species at study sites changed over the three different survey years (Kerlinger 2002).

Construction for the Munnsville Wind Farm (project) (34.5 megawatts [MW]) in Madison and Oneida Counties, New York was completed on November 1, 2007.  In accordance with the State Environmental Quality Review (SEQR) Negative Declaration and the Environmental Assessment Form for the project, post-construction monitoring was conducted during the first year following construction by Stantec Consulting (Stantec) on behalf of E.ON Climate and Renewables (E.ON)[ 2] .  The purpose of the mortality study was to investigate avian and bat mortality at the wind farm, the rate of mortality, and the possible causes of mortality.  It was the purpose of the breeding bird displacement study to investigate the level of impact to breeding birds due to development and operation of the wind farm.  The post-construction monitoring protocol, targeting potential avian and bat mortality and breeding bird displacement and avoidance was developed in 2005.  The Town of Stockbridge Planning Board served as the lead agency overseeing the project and the wildlife monitoring protocols, and the U.S. Fish and

It was determined that the bird and bat mortality study protocol would follow established and accepted procedures for monitoring collision mortality (including searches under turbines and analysis of scavenging and searcher efficiency).  The study would take place during the first year following construction of the project, and the need for additional years of survey would be dependent on the results of Year 1. ## **1.1** _**Project Area Description**_

The Munnsville Wind Farm is located in southeastern New York where the topography is characterized by steep valleys and long ridges, generally orientated north to south.  The Munnsville Wind Farm is located within the Schoharie Hills sub-ecozone of the broader Appalachian Plateau ecozone (Andrle and Carroll 1988).  The Schoharie Hills region consists of rolling uplands dissected by deep ravines.  The mean July temperature is 20° C (68° F), and the mean annual precipitation is 102 cm (40 inches [“]) (Andrle and Carroll 1988).  The Schoharie Hills sub-ecozone is approximately 47 percent forested (Andrle and Carroll 1988).  Agricultural uses (specifically dairy farming) dictate the majority of the landscape in the region.  Cultivated cropland includes corn, soybean, wheat, alfalfa, among other cover crops, and hay production.

The Munnsville Wind Farm is located in the Townships of Stockbridge, Bouckville, and Madison in Madison and Oneida Counties, New York.  The project is located east of NYS Route 46 and north of Route 20 (Figure 1).  The landscape is characterized by agricultural uplands interspersed by steep valleys.  The elevation of the Munnsville Wind Farm ranges from 456 m (1,495 ft) to 532 m (1,744 ft).  The project area is approximately 30 percent forested.  Previously harvested woodlots in the project area consist mainly of northern hardwood species such as red maple ( _Acer rubrum_ ), sugar maple ( _A. saccharum_ ), American beech ( _Fraxinus americana_ ), and oak ( _Quercus spp_ .).  The majority of the turbines are located in active agricultural fields.  Land uses in the project area mirror those in the region.  Hedgerows of trees and shrub-scrub are common between fields.

The project consists of 23[3] GE 1.5 sle turbines which have a maximum height of 119 meters (m; 389 feet [ft]) (tower and blade-tip height combined).  Seven of the 23 turbines are lit with FAA approved lighting (turbines 1, 4, 5, 14, 16, 24, and 26).  There was a temporary met tower located adjacent to turbine 22 off Trew Hill Road during the study period.

## **1.2** _**Study Area**_

The majority of the Munnsville wind turbines occur in active agricultural land.  For turbine laydown and construction, a cleared area of a 53 m (175 ft) radius around the base of all turbines was required.  At a few turbines that are closely bordered by forest, forest clearing was necessary during project construction.

Land use practices and rotational crops at each turbine location are variable among years.  The land is leased under the agreement that landowners are able to conduct normal agricultural practices up to the towers, with the exception of the very base of the towers and access drive ways.  Therefore, the only search plot management activities conducted at Munnsville during the 2008 surveys were those of the land use practices of the owners.  Vegetation growth at the base of the towers and along the access drives was periodically maintained by E.ON during the summer.

All ground cover types were searched within the 120 m by 120 m search plots with the exception of dense or steep portions of forest at the borders of some of the turbines (turbines 2, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, and 26).  The turbines included in searches, the searchable area within each search turbine plot, and a description of the habitats at all turbines in the project area is available in Table 1.  The general landowner management schedule is also included in Table 1. Half of the turbines (n=7) included in searches were located in predominantly hayfield, wheat, or oat field.  Five turbines were located in predominantly cornfield, one turbine was located in a soybean field, and one turbine was located in approximately 50 percent cornfield and 50 percent wheat field[4] .  The turbine driveways and the base of the towers consist of gravel and crushed stone.  Access driveways accounted for nearly a quarter of the search plot size at search turbines.

## **2.0 Bird and Bat Mortality Study**

## **2.1** _**Methods**_

## **2.1.1 Standardized Searches**

As outlined by the protocol developed in 2005, the bird and bat mortality surveys were conducted from April 15 to November 15, 2008.  The mortality surveys consisted of weekly searches at 12 of the 23 turbines (52 percent).  Two of the original search turbines were excluded from searches mid-season (after consultation with a NYSDEC biologist) in order to incorporate two other turbines that allowed for greater visibility during searches; however, 12 turbines total were searched during each week.  As recommended by the NYSDEC (2007), turbines included in the searches were chosen based on a random but stratified habitat approach.  Search turbines within the following land cover type categories were chosen at random: crop field (corn, soybean, and wheat), hayfield, and forest edge.

Standardized searches consisted of surveying transects established every 5 m (16 ft) within 120 m by 120 m (393 ft by 393 ft) plots centered around the 12 turbines included in the mortality searches.  The start and end points of each transect were marked along the edge of the plot (with flagging on trees or wooden stakes).  As the season progressed, stakes marking some transects at some of the search plots had to be removed in some locations due to landowner management activities.  Along transects where stakes could not be replaced, the surveyor used remaining surrounding stakes and flagging on trees to orient herself along these transects, or used the laser range finder and compass to orient herself along transects while dropping a temporary metal stake with a pink flag to mark the end of the transect she had previously searched.  When the corn and other vegetation cover types reached greater heights prior to mowing or harvesting in some plots, it became necessary to frequently use the laser range finder to find the distance to the tower or the nacelle, and compass to orient the surveyor along transects where permanent stakes and temporary dropped flags were not visible.  Thickly wooded portions at the edges of plots were excluded from the searches at turbines 12, 13, 15, and 16.

The biologist that conducted the weekly searches was well trained on survey protocols prior to beginning searches.  During a turbine plot search, the biologist would slowly walk the transects, searching on both sides of transects for bird or bat fatalities.  The surveyor would come to a stop when she needed to use the laser range finder and compass to orient herself along a transect and would then continue walking.  Any bird or bat fatality found along transects, or found as the biologist walked the 5 m-widths between transects at the north and south ends of the plots, were photographed, documented, and collected.

All intact bird or bat carcasses or remnants of scavenged carcasses (a cluster of feathers representing more than a molt, or a patch of skin and bone) were documented as fatalities.  As recommended by NYSDEC (2007), the following information was recorded for each carcass found: date, time, searcher identification, turbine number, weather conditions during the search, ground cover conditions (vegetation type and height, wet, dry, gravel, etc.), distance (determined by a laser range finder) and direction (compass) from the turbine, distance and direction from the transect from which the carcass was detected, carcass condition (fresh, rigor, decomposed, intact carcass, scavenged, feather spot, etc.), carcass position (face-up or down, sprawled out or balled up, etc.) and when possible, species, age, gender, and reproductive condition were noted.  If carcasses were found scavenged detailed notes were recorded for the purpose of scavenger identification.  Multiple photographs to document identifying

characteristics were taken of each carcass found.  Multiple Stantec biologists examined all bird and bat carcasses collected for positive identification.

Carcasses that were not found during standardized searches were documented and collected; however, these findings were not included in the estimates of annual mortality.

## **2.1.2 Dog Searches**

Additional supplemental wildlife monitoring initiated by Stantec Consulting and E.ON included dog searches to validate the results of standard searches.

A subset of turbines during each of the spring, summer, and fall seasons was searched by a biologist with a dog.  A Siberian husky with a demonstrated ability to find bird and bat carcasses was used for the surveys.  During searches, the biologist searched according to the standardized protocol by walking transects with the dog on a 1.2 m (4 ft) leash, allowing the dog to stop or move toward a carcass it detected along or adjacent to each transect.  Dog-searched turbines included those that had been searched earlier that day or previously that week by the surveyor alone.  The findings of dog searches are reported separately from the results of the standardized searches and were used to generate an alternative estimate of total bird and bat mortality.

## **2.1.3 Searcher Efficiency Trials**

During each of the spring, summer, and fall seasons, a searcher efficiency trial, unannounced to the surveyor, was conducted to estimate the percent of bird and bat carcasses that may go undetected during standardized searches.  For the trials, a secondary Stantec biologist left out carcasses early in the morning at turbines scheduled to be searched that day.  As recommended by the NYSDEC (2007), the number of carcasses used in trials was limited to avoid creating an excessive attraction to scavengers.

During trials, carcasses were placed at turbines throughout the project area within a variety of ground cover types.  Carcasses were placed within grass at a variety of heights, on bare gravel and rock, on plowed field, in cornfield, wheat field, cabbage field, and in snow.  Small, medium, and large bird carcasses and small bat carcasses were used in trials.

Carcasses were marked with tape or an elastic band, unnoticeable to the surveyor until the carcass was in hand, so that the surveyor would be able to distinguish trial carcasses.  Bat carcasses and small, medium, and large bird carcasses, at varying stages of decomposition, were placed during trials[5] .  Carcasses were placed at random within search plots.  As the surveyor searched turbines according to the standard protocol, carcasses found during the trial were collected.  After the test, the Stantec biologist collected any remaining trial carcasses to determine the number of carcasses recovered by the surveyor.

## **2.1.4 Scavenger Carcass Removal Trials**

During each season, a scavenger carcass removal trial was conducted to estimate the percent of carcasses removed by scavengers during the 7-day search intervals.  Fresh bird carcasses, including small, medium, and large bird carcasses and bat carcasses were used.  As

During trials, carcasses were placed at turbines throughout the project area within a variety of ground cover types. Therefore, the status of the carcasses on the day equivalent to the average time between impact and discovery was noted (day 4 for weekly search intervals and day 14 for seasonal dog searches). If an intact carcass remained on day 14, or if the carcass was scavenged but remained detectable to the surveyor, it was documented as not removed and was taken entirely from the search plot by the surveyor.

## **2.2** _**Statistical Analysis**_

The estimated total number of bird and bat wind farm-related fatalities is influenced by the total number of birds and bats found, the proportion of turbines searched, the percent of carcasses found by the surveyor, and the percent of carcasses removed by scavengers.  Statistical analyses were modeled after Jain _et al._ (2007, 2008).

- The results of the three scavenger trials were pooled for the trial bird and bat carcasses. The analysis considered the percent of trial birds that remained visible (including scavenged birds with substantial feather piles and flesh/bone remaining) to a surveyor on day 4 for weekly search intervals (and on day 14 for dog search intervals).  Birds that were entirely removed (including birds moved substantial distances from where they were originally placed) were considered absent.

- The results of the three searcher efficiency trails were pooled for birds and bats.  The searcher efficiency rate was determined as the total number of carcasses found divided by the total number of carcasses placed.

As described by Jain _et al._ (2007, 2008), an estimate of the total bird and bat mortality that occurred at Munnsville during the search period (ĉ) was calculated for weekly searches and for dog searches based on the number of carcasses found during each type of survey (C), the proportion of turbines searched (Ps), the percent of carcasses not removed by scavengers after the average number of days between potential impact and discovery for each search interval (Sc), and the percent of carcasses found by the surveyor (Se).

The variance was also calculated as described by Jain _et al._ (2007, 2008).

The standard deviation was then calculated based on the square root of the variance divided by the square root of the number of searched turbines, multiplied by a factor of 95 percent confidence (1.96).

There were separate estimates of annual mortality calculated based on the results of standard weekly searches and dog searches (incidental findings were not included in these estimates); however, the datasets were combined for the spatial, temporal, and species composition analysis of detected mortalities.  The results of the spatial analysis are reported in the _Discussion_ and include:

- the location of fatalities in the project area;

- the number of fatalities at turbines with varying ground cover conditions;

- the number of fatalities at turbines where the full search area could be searched verses at those few turbines where forested areas truncated search plots;

- the number of fatalities at turbines at different elevations;

- the number of fatalities at turbines in varying landscape settings (open verses bordered by forest);

- the number of fatalities at turbines in proximity to wetlands;

- the number of fatalities at turbines that are lit verse unlit; and

- the average distance of bird and bat fatalities from towers.

SAS 9.1 (SAS Institute, Inc., Cary, North Carolina) was used to compare bird and bat fatalities with several habitat and turbine characteristics.  Nonparametric tests were used in all cases to account for non-normal data.  Spearman correlations were used to test whether bird and bat fatality was linearly associated with amount of searchable area and turbine elevation.  Bat and bird fatalities were compared among turbines in open landscapes, landscapes having a partial forest edge, and landscapes bordered by a forest edge using Kruskal-Wallis tests.  Multiple pairwise comparisons using a Bonferroni adjustment were conducted to determine which pairs of landscape types had different fatality rates.  Finally, bird and bat fatalities were compared between turbines with wetlands in close proximity and turbines without, and between lit and unlit turbines, using Wilcoxon rank-sum tests.  A significance level of 0.05 was chosen prior to analysis.

## **2.3** _**Bat acoustical monitoring**_

Additional supplemental wildlife monitoring initiated by Stantec with the permission of E.ON included bat acoustical monitoring adjacent to turbines searched during the mortality study.

During the summer and fall mortality search periods, two bat detectors were deployed in the met tower (low detector at 10 m [33 ft]; high detector at 25 m [82 ft]) adjacent to search turbines 3 and 4 (Figure 2).  An additional detector was deployed in a tree (2.5 m [8 ft] near turbine 3 (Figure 2).  The Anabat II detectors (with CF Storage ZCAIM [Titley Electronics Pty Ltd.], were

deployed between June 25 and October 29.  The units were programmed to record continuously between 7:00 p.m. and 7:00 a.m on a nightly basis.

During analysis, potential call files were extracted from data files using CFCread[©] software.  Call sequences were classified to species whenever possible, based on criteria developed from review of reference calls collected by Chris Corben, the developer of the Anabat system, and other bat researchers.  However, due to similarity of call signatures between several species, all classified calls have been categorized into guilds[6] based upon similarities in call signatures. The classification scheme is as follows:

- **Unknown (UNKN)** – All call sequences with too few pulses (less than five) or of poor quality (such as indistinct pulse characteristics or background static).  These calls were further identified as either “high frequency unknown” (HFUN) for calls above 30-35 kHz (species of _myotis_ and eastern red bats [ _Lasiurus borealis_ ]) produce calls within this frequency range) or “low frequency unknown” (LFUN) for calls below 30-35 kHz (silverhaired bats ( _Lasionycteris noctivagans_ ), hoary bats ( _Lasiurus cinereus_ ), and big brown bats ( _Eptesicus fuscus_ ) produce calls within this frequency range);

- **Myotid (MYSP)** – All bats of the genus _Myotis_ .  While there are some general characteristics believed to be distinctive for several of the species in this genus, these characteristics do not occur consistently enough for any one species to be relied upon at all times when using Anabat recordings;

- **Eastern red bat/tri-colored bat (RBEP[7] )** – Eastern red bats and tri-colored bat ( _Perimyotis subflavus_ ).  These three species can produce calls distinctive only to each species.  However, significant overlap in the call pulse shape, frequency range, and slope can also occur.

- **Big brown/silver-haired bat (BBSH)** – Big brown and silver-haired bats.  These species’ call signatures commonly overlap and have therefore been included as one guild in this report.

Once all of the call files were identified and categorized in appropriate guilds, nightly tallies of detected calls were compiled.  Mean detection rates (number of calls/detector-night) for the entire sampling period were calculated for the tree detector and for the met tower detectors combined.  The periods of peak bat detector activity were compared to the timing of bat fatalities detected during the mortality study.

A HOBO data logger was deployed for 44 nights during the survey period.  The temperature data collected from the data loggers was supplemented with weather data obtained from the Rome airport, approximately 17 miles to the northeast (Weather Underground 2008).  On-site weather data was not available for the duration of the survey and comparisons with supplemental weather data should be made with caution as variation likely exists between the two locations.

Wildlife observations within the Project area indicate continued use of the site by mammalian and avian species during operation of the wind farm. The data do not suggest that FAA lighting on the lit turbines at Munnsville increases the risk of collision mortality for birds.  These results are consistent with other studies which have found no statistical differences between the number of bird and bat fatalities at lit verses unlit turbines (Jain _et al._ 2007, Arnett 2005).  The substantially higher numbers of bird fatalities observed at lit communication towers (at heights greater than 305 m [1,000 ft]) in the U.S. may be influenced by the greater heights of the towers, the guy wires, or the steady-burning lights mounted on many communication towers (Jain _et al._ 2007), verses the pulsing lights on wind turbines. Arnett _et al._ (2008) hypothesized that bats may be attracted to FAA required lights on wind turbines possibly due to attraction to insect prey, and/or because pulsing FAA red and white lights produce ultrasonic pulses.  However, other studies indicate there have been no statistically significant differences in the number of bat fatalities at lit verses unlit turbines (Arnett _et al._ 2008).

Analysis of the distance of birds and bats from the turbines included fatalities that were found scavenged and may have been moved from their original location.  The average distance of bird fatalities from the turbines was 28.6 m (93.7 ft) (this summary includes only one of the locations where the remains of the red-tailed hawk were found at turbine 12 which was the location where the majority of the carcass was found).  The maximum and minimum detected distance of a bird fatality from a tower was 50.0 m (163.9 ft) and 0.9 m (2.9 ft), respectively.  The average distance of bat fatalities from the turbines was 17.7 m (58.1 ft).  The closest distance of a bat fatality from a turbine was 0.3 m (1.0 ft) and the furthest detected distance was 41.0 m (134.4 ft).  These distances are consistent with the results of other studies which have found that majority of bird and bat carcasses fall within 60 m of the towers.  Studies conducted at

Mountaineer in West Virginia, and Myersdale in Pennsylvania determined that approximately 80 percent of fatalities are found within half the maximum distance from the height of the blade-tip to the ground (roughly 40 m) (Arnett 2005).  At the Maple Ridge Wind Power Project in New York, the fall distances were evaluated for 69 birds, of which 80 percent were within 60 m (197 ft) of the tower; and the distances were evaluated for 74 bats of which 80 percent were within 40 m (131 ft), and 98 percent were within 60 m (Jain _et al._ 2007).

## **4.3** _**Temporal Analysis**_

Bird fatalities at Munnsville were believed to occur predominantly during small-scale and localized resident bird movements due to the nature of species involved in collisions.  However, a couple of fatalities may have occurred during seasonal nighttime migration movements as these fatalities involved nocturnal migrant species and the fatalities were found within the migration season (Appendix A, Table 3).

The ruby-crowned kinglet and the red-eyed vireo were found in mid-May (May 14) and late-May (May 28), respectively.  These dates are within or at the end of the migration season and these species are nocturnal migrants (Swanson _et al._ 2008, Cimprich _et al._ 2000); therefore, the fatalities may have occurred during migration.  The fatalities of other species found were believed to occur during localized movements during the breeding season.  The song sparrow was found on August 14 prior to this species migration period.  Because wild turkeys mostly travel by walking and running, and are non-migratory (Eaton 1992), it is unknown if the wild turkeys found died as a result of collision mortality or predation.  However, female turkeys will fly when flushed (Eaton 1992) so there is a potential for collision with the turbines and therefore, the turkey fatalities were attributed to the wind farm.  Rock pigeon are non-migratory and are active during the day (Johnston 1992).  One of the rock pigeons found was scavenged so it is difficult to determine the actual cause of death; however the fatality was attributed to the wind farm.  The other pigeon was intact with the exception of some insect scavenging on the breast and was therefore suspected to have collided with the turbine.  Red-tailed hawks are active during the day and regularly forage for prey in agricultural fields (Wheeler 2003).  Both red-tailed hawks found were adults; these birds were found during the breeding season (July 16 and August 14).  They were both scavenged but due to their proximity to turbines, their deaths were believed to be the result of collision during small-scale commutes or while foraging.

The majority of bats (90 percent; n=9) were found during the late-summer/fall survey period (mid-July to end of August).  A single hoary bat was found on June 11.  The timing of the majority of fatalities of bats were consistent with other studies: a mortality study at the Maple Ridge Wind Power Project in New York found that 69.9 percent of bat fatalities occurred between July 1 and August 31 (Jain _et al._ 2007); a study at the Buffalo Mountain Wind Farm in Tennessee documented 69 percent of bat mortality between late-August and early-September (Fiedler _et al._ 2007); and, at the Mountaineer facility in West Virginia, a 6 week period from July 31 to September 11, observed a high mortality rate of 38 bats/turbine/study period (Arnett 2005).  The findings at Munnsville support the theory that most bat collisions occur during the mid-to-late summer dispersal period, and that long-distance migratory species, like the hoary bat and red bat, are at greater risk of collision.

## **4.4 Results of bat acoustic data and timing of bat fatalities**

The three Anabat detectors were deployed from June 25 to October 29, 2008 for a total of 353 detector nights.  A total of 10,718 call sequences were recorded.  The volume of calls recorded was much higher at the tree detector than at the met tower detectors combined.  The high and low met detectors operated for a combined 231 nights and recorded 465 call sequences (Appendix A, Table 9) for a detection rate of 2 calls per detector night.  The tree detector

operated for 123 nights and recorded 10,253 call sequences (Appendix A, Table 10) with a detection rate of 83 calls per detector night.  During the survey period, there were nights when detectors occasionally powered down due to a wiring malfunction or water damage to the equipment (13 potential detector nights from the three detectors combined were missed during the survey).  Appendix A, Tables 9 and 10 provide information on the number of call sequences per night, by guild and by species, recorded at the tree detector and the met tower detectors combined, as well as the weather conditions during each survey night.

Peak bat activity periods recorded at the tree detector and at the met tower detectors were variable.  There was an increase in the number of recordings at the tree detector during the third week of July.  This increase is associated with warm temperatures (Figure 6) and likely also reflects seasonal bat activity levels.  A more dramatic peak in activity recorded by the tree detector occurred during the last week of August and the first week of September.  From August 24 to August 31, 1,515 calls were recorded.  From September 1 to September 7, 1,533 calls were recorded.  A final spike in the number of calls recorded at the tree detector occurred during the last week in September (September 21 through the 28) when 1,551 call sequences were recorded.  The majority of calls sequences recorded during this week (n=1,365; 88 percent) were recorded on a single night, September 28.  During this night, mean nightly temperatures were at the top of a warming trend (17oC [63oF]) (Figure 6).  After that night, mean nightly temperatures did not reach that level for the reminder of the survey period but continued to decline.

The timing of bat fatalities at the Munnsville Wind Farm support the findings of other studies conducted at wind sites which suggest that bat fatalities most commonly occur between the end of July and the end of August (Arnett 2005, Arnett _et al._ 2008, Jain _et al._ 2007, Fiedler _et al._ 2007).  There was a relatively high detection rate recorded by the tree detector indicating high bat activity levels in the project area.  However, the mortality numbers were relatively low (as

discussed in the following section).  The results of bat detector monitoring should be interpreted in consideration of the limitations of acoustical monitoring.  Bat recordings can not be differentiated among individual bats; therefore, multiple calls from the same individual(s) may be included in the total number of calls and detection rates.

## **4.5** _**Weather Correlations**_

Due to the overall low number of fatalities, mortality data could not be statistically correlated to weather events.  In addition, there were no birds found fresh that were believed to have collided during the previous night.  There was a single bat found fresh that had collided the night before. Weather conditions for that night consisted of warm temperatures with calm to light winds and partly cloudy to overcast skies.
